decks.title: Organising — Part 1: Process, Importance and Structures
goals: Explain the meaning of organising and its four steps
Explain the importance of organising for a business
Describe functional and divisional structures with their merits and limits
Choose a suitable structure for a given business situation

slides.heading: Organising
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what organising is, its **steps**, its **importance**, and the **functional** and **divisional** structures.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what organising is, its four steps, why it matters, the functional structure and the divisional structure
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! A plan on paper does nothing by itself. Someone must decide who will do which job, with what resources, and who will report to whom. That arranging is organising, the second function of management. In this part we learn its four steps, why it matters, and the two common ways in which businesses group their work: by function and by product.

slides.heading: What is organising?
slides.body_md: **Organising** is identifying and grouping the work, assigning it to people, and fixing **authority and reporting relationships**, so that people can work together towards the plan.

nodes.label: Organising: arrange work, people and authority

visual.alt: Flow showing that organising comes after planning: planning decides what to do, organising arranges work, people and authority, and then staffing, directing and controlling follow
visual.caption: Organising turns plans into a working arrangement

slides.narration: Planning decides what is to be done. Organising decides how the work will be shared out: which activities are needed, how they are grouped, who does each one, and who has the authority to give instructions. Only after this can staffing, directing and controlling follow. So organising is the bridge between a plan and the work that carries it out.

slides.heading: The four steps of organising

visual.alt: Flow of the four steps of organising: identify and divide the work, departmentalise, assign duties, and establish reporting relationships
visual.caption: The process of organising

slides.narration: Organising follows four steps in order. First, identify all the work and divide it into manageable jobs. Second, group related jobs into departments; this is departmentalisation. Third, assign each job to a person whose skills suit it. Fourth, establish reporting relationships, so that everyone knows from whom to take orders and to whom to report. Keep this order in mind; examiners often ask you to spot a step in a case.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: organising an events company
slides.body_md: An imagined events firm in Guwahati applies the four steps.
bullets: Step 1 — List every activity and split it into jobs.
Step 2 — Group related jobs into units.
Step 3 — Match each job to a person with the right skills.
Step 4 — Fix who reports to whom.

rows: Lists venue booking, decoration, catering, sound, guest management and billing as separate jobs
Forms three units: Venue and Décor, Food, and Client Services
Gives Food to a trained chef and Client Services to an experienced coordinator
Unit staff report to unit heads; unit heads report to the owner

visual.alt: Worked example table applying the four steps of organising to an imagined events company in Guwahati: listing jobs, forming three units, assigning heads by skill, and fixing who reports to whom
visual.caption: Worked example: the four steps applied.

slides.narration: Let us watch an imagined events firm in Guwahati organise itself. It lists jobs such as venue booking, decoration, catering, sound and billing. It groups them into three units. It gives the food unit to a trained chef and client services to an experienced coordinator. Finally, unit staff report to unit heads, and unit heads report to the owner. In a case question, quote the line and name the step it shows.

slides.heading: Quick check: put the steps in order
slides.body_md: Arrange the bakery manager's actions in the correct order.
slides.narration: Think about what must come before what. You cannot group jobs until you know what the jobs are, and you cannot fix reporting lines until people have been given their jobs.

slides.heading: Why organising matters

rows: Repeating one kind of job builds skill and speed
Everyone knows whom to report to
No overlap of jobs, no idle resources
The structure can be adjusted when conditions change
Clear jobs remove confusion and duplication
Delegated work lets people grow; managers find time for new ideas
New products, branches or units can be added in an orderly way

visual.alt: Table of seven points of importance of organising: specialisation, clarity in relationships, optimum use of resources, adaptation to change, effective administration, development of personnel, and expansion and growth

slides.narration: Why do managers spend time on organising? Because it brings the benefits of specialisation, makes working relationships clear, and uses resources without waste. A good structure can also be adjusted when conditions change. Clear jobs make administration effective, delegated work helps people grow, and a sound framework lets the business expand by adding products, branches or units in an orderly way.

slides.heading: Importance in a real-looking setting
slides.body_md: In an imagined hotel in Shimla, two clerks both recorded check-ins while nobody tracked laundry.
bullets: After organising, each task had exactly **one owner**.
No duplication and no neglected task: **optimum utilisation of resources**.
Everyone knew whom to report to: **clarity in working relationships**.
slides.narration: Here is how the importance of organising shows up in practice. In an imagined hotel, two clerks were doing the same job while an important task had no owner at all. Once the work was organised, every task had one person responsible. That removed waste and confusion. In exams, link each point of importance to a line in the case rather than writing a general list.

slides.heading: Quick check: which importance?
slides.body_md: A bookshop chain moves staff to a new e-commerce team as online orders grow.
slides.narration: Ask what changed outside the firm and how the structure responded. That points to the right importance of organising.

slides.heading: Organisation structure

rows: The framework of jobs, departments and authority relationships within which work is done
Span of management: the number of subordinates one superior can manage well, which shapes the levels of the structure

visual.alt: Table explaining organisation structure: the framework of jobs, departments and authority relationships, shown in an organisation chart, shaped by the span of management, with functional and divisional as the two common forms

slides.narration: The result of organising is an organisation structure: the framework of jobs, departments and authority relationships within which work is done. It is usually shown in an organisation chart. The number of subordinates one manager can handle well, called the span of management, decides how many levels the structure needs. The two common forms you must know are the functional and the divisional structure.

visual.caption: Functional structure: jobs grouped by function (imagined firm).

slides.narration: In a functional structure, jobs are grouped by the main functions of the business: production, marketing, finance and human resources. Each department does its function for the whole firm, and each head reports to the managing director. This form suits a large business with a single product line or closely related products, where specialised knowledge in each function matters a great deal.

slides.heading: Functional structure: merits and limits
columns:
**Merits**

- Specialisation
- Little duplication
- Easy training
- Close control within a department

**Limits**

- Departmental goals over firm goals
- Hard coordination
- Conflicts between departments
- Narrow outlook

rows: Specialisation and efficiency in each function
Departments may chase their own goals over the firm's
Easy training of staff in a narrow skill set
Narrow outlook; managers get little all-round experience

visual.alt: Table of advantages of the functional structure, such as specialisation, little duplication, easy training and close control, against its limitations, such as departmental goals over firm goals, hard coordination, conflicts and a narrow outlook

slides.narration: The functional structure brings specialisation, avoids repeating the same work in many places, and makes training and control easier. But each head sees the business through one function. Departments may chase their own goals, coordinating them becomes difficult, conflicts arise, and managers do not get all-round experience. Remember both sides; questions often ask for one merit and one limitation.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the structure
slides.body_md: A production head and a marketing head of a garment exporter clash over batch sizes.
slides.narration: Which structure makes heads think mainly about their own function? That is where such clashes are common.

visual.caption: Divisional structure: jobs grouped by product (imagined group).

slides.narration: In a divisional structure, the business is split by product. Each division, such as kitchen appliances, paints or packaged foods in this imagined group, has its own production, marketing and finance, and its head reports to the chief executive. This form suits a firm with several distinct product lines, each needing different resources, technology and markets.

slides.heading: Divisional structure: merits and limits
columns:
**Merits**

- Product specialisation; varied skills for heads
- Head accountable for profit
- Quick decisions
- Easy to add a division

**Limits**

- Conflicts among divisions
- Duplication raises cost
- Divisional self-interest
- Needs many able managers

rows: Product specialisation; division heads gain varied skills
Each division head accountable for its profit
Costly: functions are duplicated in each division
Division heads may put their division before the firm
Easy to add a new division for growth

visual.alt: Table of advantages of the divisional structure, such as product specialisation, accountability for profit, quick decisions and easy growth, against its limitations, such as conflicts, duplication costs, divisional self-interest and the need for many managers

slides.narration: Because each division is like a small business, its head handles every function of one product and gains wide experience. Its profit can be measured, so the head can be held accountable. Decisions are faster, and a new product can be added as a new division. The costs are duplication of functions, competition among divisions for resources, and heads who may put their division before the firm.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choosing a structure
slides.body_md: Decide the structure for two imagined firms and give the reason.
bullets: Step 1 — Count the product lines and check whether they need different inputs and buyers.
Step 4 — Quote the case line that justifies your choice.

rows: One product (steel tubes), large output, needs specialists
Spices, coir mats and boat tours: different inputs and buyers

visual.alt: Worked example table: a single-product steel tube maker suits a functional structure, while a group selling spices, coir mats and boat tours suits a divisional structure
visual.caption: Worked example: match the structure to the business.

slides.narration: Here is a quick method. First, count the product lines. Sutlej Tubes makes only steel tubes in large volume and needs specialists, so a functional structure fits. Malabar Group sells spices, coir mats and boat tours, which need different raw materials, skills and customers, so a divisional structure fits. Always support your answer with a line from the case.

slides.heading: Functional vs divisional

rows: Hard to fix for overall results

visual.alt: Comparison table of functional and divisional structures on grouping, specialisation, responsibility for results, cost and growth

slides.narration: Here are five bases on which the two structures differ. Functional groups by function and gives functional specialisation; divisional groups by product and gives product specialisation. In a divisional firm, each head answers for the profit of a division; in a functional firm, overall responsibility is harder to fix. Functional is economical, divisional is costly, but divisional makes growth easier.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: In a divisional structure, each division's performance can be judged.
slides.narration: Think about whether a division keeps its own revenues and costs.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Arranging work, people, resources and authority to carry out plans
Divide work, departmentalise, assign duties, fix reporting lines
By function; suits a large single-product firm
By product; suits a firm with many distinct products

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of organising, its four steps, and when functional and divisional structures suit a firm

slides.narration: To sum up: organising arranges work, people, resources and authority so that plans can be carried out. Its four steps are dividing the work, departmentalising, assigning duties and fixing reporting lines. It matters for specialisation, clarity, efficient use of resources, change, administration, people and growth. A functional structure suits a large single-product firm; a divisional structure suits a firm with many distinct products.

slides.heading: Exam tips
slides.body_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing the order of the steps, or calling "assigning duties" departmentalisation.
- Choosing divisional just because a firm is large: the test is **many distinct products**.
- Writing merits of one structure as merits of the other.

**How marks are awarded**
- Case parts: quote the line **and** name the concept.
- Differences: state **both sides** on each basis.
- 5 marks: five clear points of about 20 words each.

rows: Structure named + reason from the case
One basis per point, both sides

visual.alt: Table of exam tips: for identifying a step, quote the line and name the step; for suggesting a structure, name it and give a reason from the case; for distinguishing, give one basis per point with both sides

slides.narration: A few tips before you practise. Do not confuse the steps of organising; each has a clear meaning. The choice between structures depends on the number of distinct products, not on size alone. In case questions, quote the exact line and name the concept for full marks. In difference questions, write one basis per point and state both sides.

decks.title: Organising — Part 2: Formal and Informal Organisation, Delegation and Decentralisation
goals: Compare formal and informal organisation with their merits and limits
Explain delegation and its elements: authority, responsibility and accountability

slides.heading: Organising: people and authority
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **formal and informal** organisation, **delegation** and **decentralisation**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: formal organisation, informal organisation, delegation, decentralisation, and how delegation and decentralisation differ
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome back. Every business has two organisations living side by side: the official one that management designs, and the unofficial one that grows among people who work together. In this part we compare them. Then we see how managers share authority through delegation, and how a firm can spread decision-making to every level through decentralisation.

slides.heading: Formal organisation

rows: Written rules, procedures and job descriptions

visual.alt: Table of features of formal organisation: designed by management, written rules, authority from position, and communication through the official chain

slides.narration: Formal organisation is the official structure designed by top management. It has written rules, procedures and job descriptions. Authority comes from the position a person holds, and communication travels through the official chain of command, also called the scalar chain. Its purpose is to get the organisation's work done in an orderly, predictable way.

slides.heading: Informal organisation

visual.alt: Flow showing how informal organisation arises: people work together, form friendships and shared interests, develop groups with their own norms, and pass news through the grapevine
visual.caption: How informal organisation grows

slides.narration: Informal organisation grows by itself. When people work together they make friends, share interests such as sport or music, and form groups with their own unwritten norms. News passes between them quickly and in any direction, through what is called the grapevine. No manager designs it, and it exists in every organisation.

slides.heading: Formal organisation: merits and limits
columns:
**Merits**

- Responsibility easy to fix
- No overlap of work
- Stability

**Limits**

- Slow decisions
- Rigid
- Ignores social needs

visual.alt: Table of merits of formal organisation, such as easy fixing of responsibility, no overlap and stability, against its limitations, such as slow decisions, rigidity and neglect of social needs

slides.narration: Formal organisation makes it easy to know who is responsible for what, avoids two people doing the same job, and gives stability. But following the official chain can delay decisions, the rules can be rigid, and it overlooks the human and social side of work.

slides.heading: Informal organisation: merits and limits
columns:
**Merits**

- Fast communication
- Social needs met
- Supports formal organisation

**Limits**

- Rumours
- Resistance to change
- Group norms may clash with goals

rows: Meets social needs; sense of belonging
Group norms may clash with company goals

visual.alt: Table of merits of informal organisation, such as fast communication, meeting social needs and filling gaps, against limitations, such as rumours, resistance to change and clashing group norms

slides.narration: Informal organisation spreads news quickly, gives people friendship and a sense of belonging, and helps managers learn what workers really feel. On the other hand, false rumours can travel just as fast, groups may resist change, and the norms of a group can work against company goals. Wise managers use it rather than fight it.

slides.heading: Quick check: using informal channels
slides.body_md: A production manager learns workers' views over lunch before announcing a new shift plan.
slides.narration: Which advantage of informal organisation is the manager using here?

slides.heading: Formal vs informal

visual.alt: Comparison table of formal and informal organisation on origin, authority, communication, nature and purpose

slides.narration: Compare them on five bases. Formal is created by management; informal arises from interaction. In formal, authority comes from position; in informal, from personal qualities. Formal communication follows the scalar chain; informal flows in any direction. Formal is rigid; informal is flexible. Formal serves organisational goals; informal meets the social needs of members.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: spot formal and informal
slides.body_md: Classify each line from an imagined call centre.
bullets: Step 1 — Is it laid down by management (chart, rules, portal)? **Formal**.
Step 2 — Does it arise from friendship or shared interests? **Informal**.
Step 3 — News moving faster than official channels is the **grapevine**.

headers: Line from an imagined call centre in Gurugram
rows: "Agents report to team leaders as per the chart."
"The night-shift agents share tiffin and swap tips on difficult callers."
"Leave is approved only through the HR portal."
"News of the new bonus reached every floor before the email."

Agents sharing tiffin and tips at night, and news of a bonus reaching every floor before the official email, are informal. Ask one question: was this designed by management, or did it grow among people?

slides.heading: Delegation
slides.body_md: **Delegation** is the transfer of part of a superior's **authority** to a subordinate to get a task done.

nodes.label: Manager has more work than one person can do
Assigns a task to a subordinate

visual.alt: Flow of delegation: the manager has too much work, assigns a task to a subordinate, grants matching authority, and the subordinate performs and reports back
visual.caption: Delegation in four moves

slides.narration: No manager can do all the work alone. So the manager assigns a task to a subordinate and grants enough authority to do it. The subordinate performs the task and reports back. This is delegation. Note that the manager shares authority, but does not escape answerability for the result.

slides.narration: Delegation has three elements. Authority is the right to give orders and take decisions; it flows downward. Responsibility is the obligation to do the assigned task properly; it flows upward. Accountability is answerability for the final outcome; it also flows upward and cannot be delegated. The subordinate is accountable to the manager, and the manager stays accountable to his or her own superior.

slides.body_md: Does a manager transfer accountability along with the task?

slides.heading: Why delegation matters

rows: Managers are freed for important work
Trained people can run new units
Authority relationships form the levels of management

visual.alt: Table of the importance of delegation: effective management, employee development, motivation, growth, basis of the management hierarchy, and better coordination

slides.narration: Delegation makes management effective, because managers are freed for important work. It develops employees, who learn by doing, and motivates them through trust. It supports growth, because trained people can run new units. It is the basis of the management hierarchy, and with clear authority, responsibility and accountability it improves coordination.

If it states a duty, such as keeping stock for a month, it is responsibility. If it asks the person to report or explain results, such as at a monthly review, it is accountability.

slides.heading: Decentralisation
slides.body_md: **Decentralisation**: decision-making authority is spread **systematically to all levels**, with only key decisions kept at the top. It is an **optional policy**.

slides.narration: When delegation is extended across all levels of the firm as a deliberate policy, we call it decentralisation. Lower managers decide local matters, while top management keeps key decisions such as policy and new investment. Complete centralisation or complete decentralisation is neither possible nor desirable; firms choose a balance that suits them.

slides.heading: Why decentralise?

rows: Lower managers learn to decide on their own
Decisions are taken close to the action
Units work with autonomy and can be added
Each unit's results can be judged

visual.alt: Table of the importance of decentralisation: develops initiative and managerial talent, quick decisions, relief to top management, facilitates growth and better control

slides.narration: Decentralisation develops initiative and confidence among lower managers, and prepares them for higher posts. Decisions are quicker because they are taken close to the action. Top managers get relief from routine and can focus on strategy. Units with autonomy make growth easier, and because each unit's results are visible, control can actually improve.

slides.heading: Delegation vs decentralisation

visual.alt: Comparison table of delegation and decentralisation on nature, freedom of action, status, scope and purpose

slides.narration: Learn these five differences. Delegation is compulsory, decentralisation optional. Under delegation the superior keeps more control; under decentralisation lower levels get more freedom. Delegation is a process; decentralisation is the result of a policy. Delegation is narrow in scope; decentralisation is wide. Delegation reduces a manager's burden; decentralisation increases the role of lower levels.

slides.heading: Quick check: optional or compulsory?
slides.body_md: Why is decentralisation called an optional policy decision?
slides.narration: Compare what a manager must do with what top management may choose to do.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Designed by management vs grows from social contact
Delegation spread to all levels as a policy
Neither complete centralisation nor complete decentralisation

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: formal and informal organisation, delegation, decentralisation, and the need for balance

slides.narration: To sum up: formal organisation is designed by management, while informal organisation grows from social contact, and both affect how work gets done. In delegation, authority passes down, but accountability stays with the person who delegates. Decentralisation spreads delegation to all levels as a policy, and a sensible balance with centralisation is needed.

slides.heading: Exam tips
slides.body_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying accountability can be delegated: it **cannot**.
- Writing that authority flows upward: it flows **down**; responsibility and accountability flow **up**.
- Calling any delegation "decentralisation": decentralisation covers **all levels** as a **policy**.

**How marks are awarded**
- Case parts: quote the line and name the element or concept.
- Differences: one basis per point, both sides.
- 5 marks: five points; for "evaluate", give a judgement with reasons.

rows: Delegation is compulsory; decentralisation is optional
It has merits and limits; managers can use it

visual.alt: Table of common traps: accountability is never delegated, delegation is compulsory while decentralisation is optional, and informal organisation has both merits and limits

slides.narration: Watch out for the classic traps. Accountability is never delegated. Authority flows down; responsibility and accountability flow up. Decentralisation is a policy covering all levels, not a single act of delegation. In case questions, quote the line and name the concept; in evaluation questions, state your judgement clearly and support it with reasons from the case.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and process of organising
sections.body_md:
**Organising** arranges the work, people, resources and authority needed to carry out plans. It answers: what jobs are needed, how are they grouped, who does each, and who reports to whom.

**Steps**
1. **Identification and division of work** into manageable jobs.
2. **Departmentalisation**: grouping related jobs into units (by function, product or region).
3. **Assignment of duties** to people suited by skill and training.
4. **Establishing reporting relationships**, so that authority and communication lines are clear.

key_terms.definition_md: The management function of grouping work, assigning it and fixing authority relationships to carry out plans.
Grouping similar or related jobs into units such as departments or divisions.

sections.heading: 2. Importance of organising
sections.body_md:
- **Benefits of specialisation:** repetitive work on one job builds skill and speed.
- **Clarity in working relationships:** who reports to whom is fixed.
- **Optimum utilisation of resources:** no duplication, no idle resources.
- **Adaptation to change:** the structure can be modified as conditions change.
- **Effective administration:** clear jobs remove confusion.
- **Development of personnel:** delegated work lets people grow; managers get time for innovation.
- **Expansion and growth:** new products, branches or units can be added smoothly.

sections.heading: 3. Functional and divisional structures
sections.body_md:
**Functional structure:** jobs grouped by **function** (production, marketing, finance, HR). Suits a **large firm with one product line** or closely related products needing specialists. *Merits:* specialisation, little duplication, easy training, close control. *Limits:* departmental goals over firm goals, hard coordination, conflicts, narrow outlook.

**Divisional structure:** jobs grouped by **product**; each division has its own functions. Suits a firm with **many distinct products**. *Merits:* varied skills for division heads, accountability for profit, quick decisions, easy expansion. *Limits:* conflicts over resources, duplication and high cost, divisional self-interest.

key_terms.definition_md: A structure in which jobs are grouped by the major functions of the business.
A structure in which the firm is split into product divisions, each with its own functions.

sections.heading: 4. Formal and informal organisation
sections.body_md:
**Formal organisation** is designed by top management: written rules, defined positions, authority from position, communication through the scalar chain. *Merits:* easy to fix responsibility, no overlap, stability. *Limits:* slow decisions, rigidity, neglect of social needs.

**Informal organisation** arises from social interaction: no written rules, authority from personal qualities, communication in any direction (grapevine). *Merits:* fast communication, social needs met, supports formal organisation. *Limits:* rumours, resistance to change, group norms that may clash with goals.

Both exist together; good managers use informal channels to support formal goals.

The informal channel through which news spreads quickly in any direction.

sections.heading: 5. Delegation
sections.body_md:
**Delegation** is the downward transfer of part of a superior's authority to a subordinate to perform a task. It is **compulsory** in any organisation, because no manager can do everything alone.

**Elements**
- **Authority:** right to command and decide; flows **downward**; limited by rules and laws.
- **Responsibility:** obligation to perform the task; flows **upward**.
- **Accountability:** answerability for the outcome; flows **upward**; **cannot be delegated**.

Authority should match responsibility. *Importance:* effective management, employee development, motivation, growth, basis of the hierarchy, better coordination.

key_terms.definition_md: The right of a person in a position to give orders and take decisions.
The obligation of a subordinate to perform the assigned duty.
Answerability for the final outcome; it cannot be delegated.

sections.heading: 6. Decentralisation
sections.body_md:
**Decentralisation** is the systematic spreading of decision-making authority to **all levels** of management, with only key decisions kept at the top. It is an **optional policy** decision; a **balance** with centralisation is always needed.

*Importance:* develops initiative, develops managerial talent, quick decision-making, relief to top management, facilitates growth, better control.

**Delegation vs decentralisation:** compulsory vs optional; more control vs more freedom; a process vs the result of a policy; narrow vs wide scope; reduces burden vs increases autonomy of lower levels.

Keeping decision-making authority mainly with top management.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up the steps of organising, or treating assignment of duties as departmentalisation.
- Choosing a divisional structure only because the firm is big: look for **several distinct products**.
- Saying accountability can be delegated (it cannot), or that authority flows upward (it flows down).
- Treating decentralisation as a single act: it is a **policy** covering all levels.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, or a concept named.
- Case parts: quote the line **and** name the concept.
- 3 marks: three points with brief explanation (about 50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five clear points or bases (about 80–120 words); differences state both sides on each basis.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes **organising** as a function of management?

options.text_md: Deciding in advance what is to be done and how it is to be done
Arranging activities, people and resources and setting up authority relationships so that plans can be carried out
Comparing actual performance with standards and correcting deviations
Guiding, motivating and supervising employees at work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Arranging activities, people and resources and setting up authority relationships so that plans can be carried out. Organising puts plans into action by grouping work, assigning it and fixing who reports to whom. Deciding in advance is planning, comparing with standards is controlling, and guiding employees is directing.

questions.stem_md: Which is the **first** step in the process of organising?

options.text_md: Departmentalisation
Assignment of duties
Establishing reporting relationships
Identification and division of work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Identification and division of work. The total work is first identified and split into manageable jobs; only then can similar jobs be grouped (departmentalisation), duties assigned and reporting lines fixed.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined furniture firm in Jodhpur groups all carving, polishing and assembly jobs under a "Production" unit and all showroom and online-order jobs under a "Sales" unit. Which step of organising is she performing?

options.text_md: Departmentalisation
Identification and division of work
Assignment of duties
Establishing reporting relationships

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Departmentalisation. Grouping similar jobs into units such as Production and Sales is departmentalisation. Dividing the work into jobs comes before it, and naming people for jobs and fixing who reports to whom come after it.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined courier start-up in Kochi, the founder announces that the four delivery supervisors will report to the operations manager, who in turn will report to her. Which step of organising does this show?

options.text_md: Departmentalisation
Assignment of duties
Establishing reporting relationships
Identification and division of work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Establishing reporting relationships. Deciding who reports to whom builds the chain of authority, which is the step of establishing reporting relationships.

questions.stem_md: After creating a Quality Control department, the manager of an imagined spice-packing unit in Guntur appoints Lakshmi, a food technologist, to head it because of her training. Which step of organising is this?

options.text_md: Departmentalisation
Establishing reporting relationships
Assignment of duties
Identification and division of work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Assignment of duties. Giving a defined job to a person suited to it by skill and training is assignment of duties.

questions.stem_md: When each worker in a firm repeatedly does one part of the total work, skill and speed improve. Which benefit of organising does this describe?

options.text_md: Benefits of specialisation
Adaptation to change
Development of personnel
Expansion and growth

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Benefits of specialisation. Repeating one kind of work builds skill and speed, which is the benefit of specialisation that comes from dividing work systematically.

questions.stem_md: An imagined hotel in Shimla found that two clerks were both recording guest check-ins while nobody tracked laundry. After the work was reorganised, each task had exactly one owner. Which importance of organising is shown?

options.text_md: Adaptation to change
Development of personnel
Expansion and growth
Optimum utilisation of resources

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Optimum utilisation of resources. Removing duplication of work and covering the neglected task means people and time are used fully and without waste: optimum utilisation of resources.

questions.stem_md: When online orders overtook walk-in sales, an imagined bookshop chain in Pune shifted staff from shop counters to a new e-commerce team without disturbing the rest of the business. Which importance of organising does this reflect?

options.text_md: Benefits of specialisation
Adaptation to change
Clarity in working relationships
Effective administration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Adaptation to change. A sound organisation structure can be modified when the environment changes, so the firm adjusts roles to new conditions: adaptation to change.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Departmentalisation can be done only after the total work has been divided into jobs.

**Reason (R):** Departmentalisation means grouping similar or related jobs into units.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since departmentalisation groups jobs, the jobs must first exist, that is, the work must already have been identified and divided.

questions.stem_md: True or false? By fixing who reports to whom, organising brings clarity in working relationships and helps fix responsibility.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Clear reporting lines tell each person from whom to take orders and to whom to report, so responsibility for each task can be fixed.

questions.stem_md: Grouping similar and related jobs into units such as purchase, production and sales is called ___.
questions.solution_md: This step is departmentalisation: related jobs are grouped into departments.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps that the manager of an imagined bakery in Indore follows while organising, in the correct order.

options.text_md: Groups related jobs into Production and Sales departments
Decides that bakers report to the head baker and the head baker to the owner
Lists all the work and splits it into jobs such as kneading, baking, packing and selling
Gives each job to a suitable person

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). Identification and division of work comes first, then departmentalisation, then assignment of duties, and finally establishing reporting relationships.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is meant by organising? Why is it called the means of putting plans into action?
questions.solution_md: Meaning with its elements, then the link with implementing plans.

answer.model_answer_md: **Organising** is identifying and grouping the work, assigning it to people and fixing **authority and reporting relationships**. Plans state what is to be done; organising arranges **who will do what, with which resources**, so it turns plans into action.

questions.stem_md: An imagined textile mill in Surat assigns dyeing, weaving and printing to separate trained teams. Explain the importance of organising shown here.
questions.solution_md: Name the benefit and explain how repetition of one task raises efficiency.

answer.model_answer_md: This shows the **benefits of specialisation**. Each team does one kind of work again and again, so it gains **skill and speed**, makes fewer errors and the mill produces more output with the same effort.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three steps in the process of organising, using an imagined school canteen as your example.
questions.solution_md: Any three of the four steps, each explained and linked to the canteen.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Identification and division of work:** the canteen manager lists all work (buying, cooking, serving, cleaning) and splits it into jobs.
2. **Departmentalisation:** related jobs are grouped, e.g. a kitchen unit and a service counter.
3. **Establishing reporting relationships:** cooks report to the head cook and counter staff to the supervisor, who reports to the manager.

questions.stem_md: State three ways in which organising helps a growing business.
questions.solution_md: Any three points of importance, each with a brief explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Clarity in working relationships:** everyone knows whom to report to, so communication and responsibility are clear.
2. **Optimum utilisation of resources:** jobs are fixed without overlap, so people, money and machines are not wasted.
3. **Expansion and growth:** a sound structure lets the firm add branches, products or departments in an orderly way.

questions.stem_md: Ritika is setting up an imagined online tutoring company in Bhopal with 40 tutors and 10 support staff. Explain the steps she should follow to organise the company and state one benefit she can expect.
questions.solution_md: The four steps applied to the company, plus one relevant benefit.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Identify and divide the work:** list all activities (teaching, scheduling, technical support, billing, marketing) and split them into jobs.
2. **Departmentalise:** group related jobs into units such as Academics, Technology, Accounts and Marketing.
3. **Assign duties:** give each job to a person suited to it, e.g. the maths tutors to Academics and an engineer to Technology.
4. **Establish reporting relationships:** decide that tutors report to subject heads and heads report to Ritika, so authority is clear.
5. **Benefit:** with work divided and lines clear, the company gains **specialisation** and **clarity in working relationships**, and can grow by adding new subjects without confusion.

questions.stem_md: In a **functional structure**, activities are grouped on the basis of

options.text_md: the major functions such as production, marketing, finance and human resources
the different products made by the firm
the regions in which the firm sells
the personal friendships among employees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the major functions such as production, marketing, finance and human resources. A functional structure groups jobs by function. Grouping by product is the divisional structure; friendships give rise to informal organisation.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company in Ludhiana makes only one product, bicycle chains, but its operations are large and need specialised staff. Which structure suits it best?

options.text_md: Divisional structure
Functional structure
Informal structure
No structure, as the firm makes only one product

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Functional structure. A large firm with a single product line and a need for specialisation suits a functional structure. A divisional structure is meant for firms with several distinct products.

questions.stem_md: An imagined group in Chennai makes cement, packaged tea and solar panels, each needing its own production methods and marketing. Which structure is most suitable?

options.text_md: Functional structure
Informal structure
Divisional structure
A single department for all three products

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Divisional structure. Several unrelated product lines, each with its own technology and market, call for a divisional structure in which each product forms a separate division.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **limitation** of the divisional structure?

options.text_md: Functional heads stress their own department over the goals of the firm
It cannot be used by a firm with many product lines
Profit of each product cannot be measured
Each division sets up its own functions, so activities and costs are duplicated

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Each division sets up its own functions, so activities and costs are duplicated. Because every division has its own production, marketing and finance, the same activities are repeated, which raises costs. Stress on departmental goals is a limitation of the functional structure; the divisional form suits many product lines and makes profit per product easy to measure.

questions.stem_md: Which advantage is associated with the **functional** structure?

options.text_md: Each division head is accountable for the profit of a product
New product lines can be added without disturbing existing ones
Heads gain experience of all functions of one product
Minimal duplication of effort, since each function is performed in one department

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Minimal duplication of effort, since each function is performed in one department. In a functional structure each function is concentrated in one department, so work is not repeated. The other three are advantages of the divisional structure.

questions.stem_md: The board of an imagined appliance maker in Noida wants to know exactly how profitable its fans, coolers and water heaters each are, and to hold one manager answerable for each. Which structure helps most?

options.text_md: Functional structure
Informal structure
Divisional structure
Centralised functional structure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Divisional structure. In a divisional structure each product division has its own revenue and costs, so its profit can be measured and its head held accountable.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined garment exporter in Tiruppur, the production head insists on long runs of one design to cut costs while the marketing head wants many small batches of new designs. This conflict is typical of which structure?

options.text_md: Divisional structure
Functional structure
Informal organisation
Decentralised organisation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Functional structure. In a functional structure each head looks at goals from the view of one function, so conflicts between departments and difficulty in coordination are common.

questions.stem_md: An imagined food company in Nagpur plans to launch a frozen-snacks line next year and wants to add it without upsetting its existing biscuit and juice businesses. Which structure makes this easiest?

options.text_md: Divisional structure
Functional structure
Informal organisation
A structure without reporting relationships

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Divisional structure. A divisional structure allows a new division to be added for a new product without disturbing existing divisions, which supports expansion.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Coordination across departments may become difficult in a functional structure.

**Reason (R):** Each functional head tends to give more importance to the objectives of his or her own department.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: when heads chase departmental goals, the departments pull apart and coordinating them becomes harder.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A divisional structure can be costly to run.

**Reason (R):** A divisional structure helps in developing varied skills in the head of a division.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The cost comes from duplication of functions in every division; developing varied skills is a separate advantage.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a divisional structure, the performance of each division can be judged because its revenues and costs are separately known.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Each division works like a separate unit with its own revenues and costs, so its profit and performance can be assessed and its head held accountable.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature of an organisation structure with the structure it belongs to.

options.text_md: Grouping of jobs by product lines
Grouping of jobs by major functions
Arises from social interaction among employees
Deliberately designed, with official rules and positions

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Product-wise grouping is divisional; function-wise grouping is functional; networks from social contact are informal; a structure deliberately set by management is formal.

questions.stem_md: What is a functional structure? Name the kind of business for which it is suitable.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus suitability.

answer.model_answer_md: A **functional structure** groups jobs of a similar nature into departments by **function**, such as production, marketing, finance and personnel, each reporting to a head. It suits a **large firm with a single or closely related product line** that needs specialisation.

questions.stem_md: What is a divisional structure? When should a firm adopt it?
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus suitability.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **divisional structure** the organisation is split into **divisions by product**, and each division has its own production, marketing and finance. A firm should adopt it when it has **many distinct product lines**, each needing its own resources and expertise.

questions.stem_md: State three advantages of a functional structure for a large single-product manufacturer.
questions.solution_md: Any three advantages of the functional structure, each briefly explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Specialisation:** each department focuses on one function, so staff become experts and efficiency rises.
2. **Less duplication:** each function is done in one place, so effort and cost are not repeated.
3. **Easier training and control:** staff in one department need training in a narrow set of skills, and the head can supervise them closely.

questions.stem_md: An imagined consumer-goods group in Kolkata is thinking of moving to a divisional structure. Explain three problems it should be ready for.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations of the divisional structure, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Conflict among divisions:** divisions may compete for funds, staff and attention from top management.
2. **Higher cost:** each division needs its own production, marketing and finance, so activities are duplicated.
3. **Divisional self-interest:** powerful division heads may favour their own division and ignore the interests of the group as a whole.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between functional and divisional structures on any five bases.
questions.solution_md: Five bases with both sides stated on each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Basis of grouping:** functional groups jobs by **function**; divisional groups them by **product**.
2. **Specialisation:** functional gives **functional** specialisation; divisional gives **product** specialisation.
3. **Responsibility for results:** in functional it is hard to fix responsibility for overall performance; in divisional each **division head is accountable for profit**.
4. **Cost:** functional is **economical** as there is no duplication; divisional is **costly** because each division repeats the functions.
5. **Coordination and growth:** coordination is **difficult across** functional departments; in divisional it is easier within a division, and new divisions can be added for **expansion**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company in Ahmedabad makes paints, adhesives and cosmetics. Advise it, with five reasons, whether a divisional structure would suit it.
questions.solution_md: Clear recommendation with five reasons linked to the case; a note on cost is good practice.

answer.model_answer_md:
A **divisional structure** would suit the company because:
1. **Distinct products:** paints, adhesives and cosmetics need different technologies, suppliers and markets, so each can form a division.
2. **Accountability:** each division head can be held responsible for that division's **profit**, so weak units are spotted early.
3. **Quick decisions:** divisions have autonomy and can respond fast to their own customers.
4. **Managerial development:** division heads handle all functions of a product, preparing them for top posts.
5. **Growth:** a new product line can be added as a new division without disturbing the others. The firm should, however, guard against **duplication of costs**.

questions.stem_md: Which is a feature of **formal** organisation?

options.text_md: It arises on its own from friendships among employees
It is deliberately designed by top management to achieve organisational goals
Communication flows in any direction without fixed channels
It has no written rules or procedures

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is deliberately designed by top management to achieve organisational goals. Formal organisation is consciously created by management with defined positions and rules. The other three describe informal organisation.

questions.stem_md: Informal organisation emerges mainly from

options.text_md: the official organisation chart
the rules laid down by the board of directors
government regulation of companies
social interaction among people working together

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** social interaction among people working together. When people work together they form friendships and groups based on shared interests; this network is the informal organisation.

questions.stem_md: The web of channels through which news passes from person to person in an informal organisation, in any direction, is known as the

options.text_md: grapevine
scalar chain
chain of command
span of management

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** grapevine. Informal communication spreads like a grapevine: fast, in all directions, and without following the official chain. Scalar chain and chain of command belong to formal communication.

questions.stem_md: Staff of an imagined bank branch in Mysuru who play cricket together on Sundays often solve work problems over tea without waiting for official meetings. This illustrates

options.text_md: formal organisation
divisional structure
informal organisation
decentralisation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** informal organisation. A group formed through a shared hobby, with communication outside official channels, is informal organisation.

questions.stem_md: Which is a **limitation** of formal organisation?

options.text_md: Rumours spread quickly and cannot be controlled
It is difficult to fix responsibility
Decisions may be delayed because the official chain of command must be followed
It has no stable rules

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Decisions may be delayed because the official chain of command must be followed. Following the scalar chain can slow decisions. Rumours are a limitation of informal organisation, and formal organisation actually makes it easy to fix responsibility and gives stability.

questions.stem_md: The production manager of an imagined pharma unit in Baddi uses lunch-time conversations to learn how workers feel about a new shift plan before announcing it. Which advantage of informal organisation is she using?

options.text_md: It gives quick feedback and fills gaps in formal communication
It makes responsibility easy to fix
It ensures unity of command
It provides a written procedure for every task

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It gives quick feedback and fills gaps in formal communication. Informal channels carry views quickly and help managers understand workers, complementing formal communication. Fixing responsibility, unity of command and written procedures are features of formal organisation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Informal organisation can sometimes harm a business.

**Reason (R):** False rumours can spread quickly through informal channels.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: misleading news spreads fast through the grapevine and can create fear or resistance, which is one way informal organisation can harm the firm.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Formal organisation gives stability to an organisation.

**Reason (R):** Formal organisation is flexible because it has no fixed rules.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: well-defined rules and positions make behaviour predictable, which gives stability. R is false: formal organisation has fixed rules and is often criticised for rigidity.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Informal organisation is created through written rules and an official chart prepared by management.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Informal organisation has no written rules or official chart; it grows out of personal and social relationships. Written rules belong to formal organisation.

questions.stem_md: What is informal organisation? Give one example from an imagined office.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus a suitable example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Informal organisation** is the network of **personal and social relationships** that forms when people work together, outside the official structure. Example: clerks of an imagined insurance office in Lucknow who share lunch daily and pass on news to one another.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three advantages of informal organisation for a firm.
questions.solution_md: Any three advantages, each briefly explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Faster communication:** news travels quickly because it need not follow the chain of command.
2. **Social needs met:** workers find friendship and a sense of belonging, which raises job satisfaction.
3. **Support to formal organisation:** managers learn workers' real views through informal channels, which helps them plan and fill gaps in formal communication.

questions.stem_md: Give two advantages of formal organisation.
questions.solution_md: Any two advantages, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Easy to fix responsibility:** each position has defined duties and a clear superior, so it is known who is answerable.
2. **Stability and no overlap:** rules and procedures make behaviour predictable and prevent two people doing the same work.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate between formal and informal organisation on any five bases.
questions.solution_md: Five bases with both sides on each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** formal is the **official structure** of roles and authority; informal is the **network of social relationships** among employees.
2. **Origin:** formal is **deliberately created** by management; informal **arises on its own** from interaction.
3. **Authority:** in formal it comes from **position**; in informal it comes from **personal qualities** and acceptance by the group.
4. **Communication:** formal follows the **scalar chain**; informal flows freely in **any direction** (grapevine).
5. **Nature and purpose:** formal is **rigid** and aims at organisational goals; informal is **flexible** and meets members' social needs.

questions.stem_md: Delegation of authority means

options.text_md: a subordinate taking over all the authority of the superior
the superior giving up all responsibility for the work
spreading authority to every level of the firm as a policy
a superior passing part of his or her authority to a subordinate to get a task done

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a superior passing part of his or her authority to a subordinate to get a task done. Delegation is the downward transfer of some authority from a superior to a subordinate for a task. The superior does not give up responsibility or accountability, and spreading authority to all levels as a policy is decentralisation.

questions.stem_md: Which element of delegation **cannot be passed on** to a subordinate?

options.text_md: Authority
Accountability
Responsibility for doing the assigned work
The task itself

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Accountability. The superior stays answerable to his or her own superior for the final result even after delegating, so accountability cannot be delegated.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the elements of delegation is correct?

options.text_md: Authority flows downward, while responsibility and accountability flow upward
Authority flows upward, while responsibility flows downward
All three flow downward
Accountability flows downward from the superior

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Authority flows downward, while responsibility and accountability flow upward. A superior grants authority downward; the subordinate is responsible and answerable upward to the superior.

questions.stem_md: Ananya, sales manager at an imagined mobile-phone retailer in Hyderabad, allows her assistant Kabir to approve discounts up to five per cent for bulk buyers and tells him to report every such deal to her at week end. Which element of delegation is shown by "allows Kabir to approve discounts"?

options.text_md: Responsibility
Authority
Accountability
Decentralisation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Authority. The right to take a decision (approve discounts) is authority. Reporting the deals at week end reflects accountability.

questions.stem_md: Why is decentralisation described as an **optional policy decision**, unlike delegation?

options.text_md: Decentralisation is required by law while delegation is not
Delegation is never needed in small firms
Top management chooses how far to spread authority to lower levels, whereas no manager can do all work alone without delegating
Decentralisation applies only to government offices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Top management chooses how far to spread authority to lower levels, whereas no manager can do all work alone without delegating. Delegation is necessary because a manager cannot do all the work alone; decentralisation is a deliberate choice by top management about how much authority to push down to all levels.

questions.stem_md: An imagined supermarket chain lets each of its 30 store managers across Maharashtra decide local stock, staff rosters and festival offers, while head office sets only overall policy. This is an example of

options.text_md: centralisation
informal organisation
functional structure
decentralisation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** decentralisation. Systematically spreading decision-making authority to lower levels (store managers) across the organisation, with only key decisions kept at the top, is decentralisation.

questions.stem_md: The founder of an imagined travel company in Jaipur now spends her time on new markets because branch heads handle daily decisions. Which importance of decentralisation does this show?

options.text_md: Develops initiative among subordinates
Better control
Quick decision-making at lower levels
Relief to top management

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Relief to top management. The focus of the case is that the founder is freed from routine decisions and can concentrate on strategy: relief to top management. The other benefits exist but are not what the situation highlights.

questions.stem_md: Responsibility in delegation means

options.text_md: the right to give orders and take decisions
the answerability of the superior to the board
the obligation of a subordinate to perform the duty assigned properly
the formal transfer of ownership of the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the obligation of a subordinate to perform the duty assigned properly. Responsibility is the duty to carry out the assigned task. The right to give orders is authority, and being answerable for results is accountability.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A manager remains accountable for a task even after delegating it.

**Reason (R):** Accountability cannot be delegated.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since accountability cannot be passed on, the manager is still answerable for the result of the delegated task.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Delegation and decentralisation have the same scope.

**Reason (R):** Decentralisation is the extension of delegation to the lowest levels of the organisation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: delegation has a narrow scope (one superior and subordinate), while decentralisation is wide (all levels). R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A subordinate should be given authority matching the responsibility assigned.

**Reason (R):** Authority flows downward in an organisation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A holds because without enough authority a subordinate cannot complete the task (and too much invites misuse); R only states the direction in which authority flows.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a manager delegates a task, he or she also transfers accountability for its result to the subordinate.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Authority is delegated, but accountability cannot be; the manager remains answerable to his or her superior.

questions.stem_md: The answerability of a subordinate for the final outcome of an assigned task is called ___.
questions.solution_md: Being answerable for the outcome is accountability; it is enforced through regular reporting.

questions.stem_md: Match each line from an imagined hospital administrator's instructions to the element or concept it shows.

options.text_md: "You may order medicines up to the approved budget."
"It is your duty to keep the pharmacy stocked."
"Send me a stock report every Friday."
"All ward heads across our six hospitals will now take such decisions."

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The right to order is authority; the duty to keep stock is responsibility; reporting for the outcome is accountability; extending decision-making to all ward heads across units is decentralisation.

questions.stem_md: Define delegation and state why it is needed in a large organisation.
questions.solution_md: Definition plus one reason for need.

answer.model_answer_md: **Delegation** is the transfer of part of a superior's **authority** to a subordinate to perform an assigned task. It is needed because in a large organisation no manager can do all the work alone; delegation lets work be **shared** while the manager focuses on more important tasks.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between authority and responsibility on two bases.
questions.solution_md: Two bases with both sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** authority is the **right to command** and decide; responsibility is the **obligation to perform** the assigned duty.
2. **Direction of flow:** authority flows **downward** from superior to subordinate; responsibility flows **upward** from subordinate to superior.

questions.stem_md: What is decentralisation? Is complete decentralisation desirable?
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus the need for balance.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **decentralisation**, top management deliberately pushes **decision-making authority down to every level**, keeping only major decisions such as policy for itself. **Complete** decentralisation is not desirable, because top management must keep control of policy; a **balance** with centralisation is needed.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which delegation benefits an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Any three points of importance of delegation, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Effective management:** managers are freed from routine work and can focus on planning and important decisions.
2. **Employee development:** subordinates get chances to use their skills and grow into future managers.
3. **Motivation:** trust shown through delegated authority gives subordinates confidence and a sense of recognition, so they work better.

questions.stem_md: An imagined restaurant chain with 25 outlets in South India wants to decentralise. Explain three benefits it can expect.
questions.solution_md: Three benefits linked to the restaurant chain.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Quick decisions:** outlet managers can change menus or staff rosters on the spot without waiting for head office.
2. **Develops managerial talent:** outlet managers gain decision-making experience and can be promoted to regional posts.
3. **Facilitates growth:** each outlet works with some autonomy, so the chain can open new outlets and judge each one by its results.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between delegation and decentralisation on any five bases.
questions.solution_md: Five bases with both sides on each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Nature:** delegation is a **compulsory** act, as no manager can do all work alone; decentralisation is an **optional policy** decision of top management.
2. **Freedom of action:** under delegation the superior keeps **more control**; under decentralisation lower levels get **more freedom**.
3. **Status:** delegation is a **process**; decentralisation is the **result** of a policy that extends delegation.
4. **Scope:** delegation is **narrow**, between a superior and subordinate; decentralisation is **wide**, covering all levels.
5. **Purpose:** delegation aims to **reduce the burden** of the manager; decentralisation aims to **increase the role and autonomy** of lower levels.

questions.stem_md: The new CEO of an imagined engineering firm in Pune says, "Every purchase above ₹5,000 must come to my desk." Evaluate this approach and explain four benefits the firm would gain by decentralising instead.
questions.solution_md: A reasoned judgement on over-centralisation, then four benefits of decentralisation linked to the firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Evaluation:** keeping all such decisions at the top causes **delays**, overloads the CEO and stops managers from learning; some balance is needed, so only major decisions should stay with the CEO.
**Benefits of decentralising:**
1. **Quick decision-making:** managers close to the work can buy what they need without waiting.
2. **Relief to top management:** the CEO gets time for strategy and growth.
3. **Develops initiative and talent:** managers learn to take decisions and become ready for higher posts.
4. **Better control and growth:** each unit's performance can be judged and the firm can expand with self-reliant units.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined company, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Heads for production, purchase, sales and accounts point to a functional structure.

**(b)** Several distinct products with different inputs and markets call for divisions.

**(c) (i)** Two reasons tied to lines of the passage.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two limitations of the divisional structure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Functional structure**: one head for each function for the whole company.

**(b)** **Divisional structure**, with separate divisions for cattle feed, organic fertiliser and dairy products.

questions.stem_md: How does organising lead to **effective administration**?

options.text_md: By removing the need for managers
By clearly describing jobs and related duties, it avoids confusion and duplication
By letting every employee decide his or her own duties
By fixing prices of the firm's products

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** By clearly describing jobs and related duties, it avoids confusion and duplication. Clear job descriptions and authority relationships remove confusion and overlap, which makes administration effective.

questions.stem_md: Why does a divisional structure help develop managers for top positions?

options.text_md: A division head handles all functions of a product and so gains varied experience
Division heads perform only one function
Division heads have no authority
It removes the need for a chief executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A division head handles all functions of a product and so gains varied experience. Managing production, marketing and finance of one product gives a division head broad skills needed for top management.
